title: Time-MoE: sizing a dense baseline
specification: Our decoder-only transformer employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer as a substitute for the standard feed-forward network (FFN). The MoE layer comprises N=8 non-shared expert FFNs plus one shared expert FFN. For each token, a top-k gating mechanism activates K=2 non-shared experts, while the shared expert is always applied. To evaluate the performance and efficiency benefits of sparse architectures in time series forecasting, we replaced the MoE layer with a dense layer containing an equivalent number of parameters as the activated parameters in the MoE layer.
full_specification: Our decoder-only transformer employs a mixture-of-experts (MoE) layer as a substitute for the standard feed-forward network (FFN). The MoE layer comprises N=8 non-shared expert FFNs plus one shared expert FFN. For each token, a top-k gating mechanism activates K=2 non-shared experts, while the shared expert is always applied. To evaluate the performance and efficiency benefits of sparse architectures in time series forecasting, we replaced the MoE layer with a dense layer containing an equivalent number of parameters as the activated parameters in the MoE layer. Using identical training data and configurations, we train three dense models matching the sizes of the three TIME-MOE variants. The forecasting quality is then compared on zero-shot benchmarks. The TIME-MOE architecture is a decoder-only transformer that operates in an autoregressive manner. Input time series are point-wise tokenized and encoded. Each transformer block includes causal multi-head self-attention and the MoE layer described above, followed by residual connections and RMSNorm. The models are pre-trained on Time-300B, a large-scale dataset spanning nine domains. The dense baselines are constructed to assess sparsity benefits, with the dense FFN sized to match the activated parameters in the MoE layer. The dense and sparse models are trained with identical data and hyperparameters, and their zero-shot forecasting performance is evaluated on six benchmark datasets.
blocker: “Activated parameters” leaves the counting scope unresolved: the experts used per token, or every expert in the MoE layer?
readiness_reason: The counting scope determines the dense FFN size. Choosing a different expert set changes the baseline and the intended capacity-matched comparison.
clarification: What exactly constitutes the 'activated parameters' when sizing the dense baseline? Should the dense FFN have the same number of parameters as the shared expert plus the two activated non-shared experts per token, or as the total parameters of all experts?
evidence: Author response specifying that activated parameters are the parameters of the shared expert and the K=2 selected non-shared experts per token.
reference: To compare sparse MoE models against dense baselines under equal capacity, we construct a dense baseline by replacing the Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer with a single feed-forward network (FFN). The dense FFN is sized to have exactly the same number of parameters as the total parameters actively used per token during the MoE forward pass. Specifically, the MoE layer consists of one shared expert FFN and N=8 non-shared expert FFNs. For each token, only K=2 non-shared experts are gated by the top-2 router, and their outputs are combined with the shared expert's output. Hence, the parameters consumed per token are those of the shared expert plus the two selected non-shared experts. The dense baseline FFN must be configured to have a parameter count equal to the sum of the shared expert's parameters and twice the individual non-shared expert's parameters (since two are selected). For example, in the base model each expert FFN uses a SwiGLU structure with input dimension d_model=384, intermediate dimension d_ff=1536, and output dimension d_model=384. The dense baseline FFN employs the same structure but with an inner dimension scaled so that its total parameters match the activated parameter total of 50M for the entire model, not the total MoE parameter count of 113M. This ensures a fair, capacity-matched comparison between the sparse MoE and dense architectures across all model scales.

title: XFeat: the missing keypoint classifier
specification:
We propose XFeat, a lightweight local feature extractor for efficient image matching on resource-constrained hardware.

[…]

The keypoint head operates in parallel on the input image by unfolding it into an 8×8 cell grid and processing this grid with lightweight convolutions to predict keypoint locations.
full_specification: We propose XFeat, a lightweight local feature extractor for efficient image matching on resource-constrained hardware. The goal is to maintain competitive accuracy while enabling fast CPU‑only inference. The model takes an RGB image and produces sparse keypoints with descriptors, a dense reliability map, and a semi‑dense matching output via a coarse‑to‑fine refinement module. A six‑block convolutional backbone progressively reduces spatial resolution, while a single skip connection feeds a downsampled input projection into the 1/4‑resolution block. The descriptor head fuses multi‑scale features from resolutions 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 using bilinear upsampling and 1×1 convolutions, followed by a fusion block and a reliability prediction head. The keypoint head operates in parallel on the input image by unfolding it into an 8×8 cell grid and processing this grid with lightweight convolutions to predict keypoint locations. A separate fine matcher takes concatenated descriptor pairs and predicts cell offsets for coarse‑to‑fine matching. Training uses a mixture of Megadepth and COCO images, combined with a dual‑softmax descriptor loss, a reliability loss, a fine matching loss, and a keypoint distillation loss.
blocker: The keypoint head omits the final 1×1 classifier that produces 65 logits per cell: 64 within-cell positions and one dustbin class.
readiness_reason: The description does not determine the output layer that converts the keypoint features into the required per-cell predictions.
clarification: What is the exact layer that produces the 65 logits per cell in the keypoint head? How is the output dimensionality achieved from the unfolded 8×8 grid?
evidence: Examine the model implementation in the official code repository (specifically the keypoint head forward pass) to determine the convolution layers used after unfolding.
reference: We propose a lightweight local feature extractor, XFeat, for efficient image matching on resource-constrained hardware, aiming to deliver competitive accuracy with fast CPU inference. The model processes an RGB image through a six‑block convolutional backbone (channels {4,8,24,64,64,128}, each block a Conv‑BN‑ReLU) with a single skip connection that injects a downsampled input projection into the 1/4‑resolution block. A multi‑scale descriptor head fuses features from 1/8, 1/16, and 1/32 scales via bilinear upsampling and 1×1 convolutions; the fused output is refined by a fusion block and then split into a dense descriptor map and a reliability heatmap. The keypoint head operates in parallel by unfolding the input image into 8×8 cells and applying lightweight 1×1 convolutions to produce 65 logits per cell, corresponding to 64 cell‑position classes and one dustbin class, thereby yielding a sparse set of keypoint detections. A fine matcher, implemented as a lightweight MLP, receives concatenated descriptor pairs and predicts pixel‑level offsets for semi‑dense matching. Training uses a mixture of Megadepth and COCO images (6:4 ratio, resized to ~800×600) with four losses: a dual‑softmax descriptor loss, a reliability loss, a fine matching loss, and a keypoint distillation loss from ALIKE. Optimization uses Adam with an initial learning rate of 3e‑4 and exponential decay by 0.5 every 30k iterations, with a batch size of 10 image pairs.

title: PGExplainer: paper and code disagree
specification: We propose a parameterized explainer, PGExplainer, to provide global explanations for predictions made by graph neural networks. For node classification tasks, we first train a GNN model on a given graph dataset. The GNN consists of three consecutive graph convolutional layers that feed directly into a fully connected classification layer. Each convolutional layer propagates messages along edges and updates node representations. We then train PGExplainer to generate edge importance weights by maximizing mutual information between the original GNN prediction and predictions obtained from sampled subgraphs. The explainer network uses the node embeddings from the trained GNN to compute edge weights, enabling collective explanation across multiple nodes. Explanations are evaluated on synthetic datasets with known ground-truth motifs.

We then train PGExplainer to generate edge importance weights by maximizing mutual information between the original GNN prediction and predictions obtained from sampled subgraphs. The explainer network uses the node embeddings from the trained GNN to compute edge weights, enabling collective explanation across multiple nodes. Explanations are evaluated on synthetic datasets with known ground-truth motifs.
blocker: The paper describes sequential GCN layers feeding the classifier, but the released model concatenates the intermediate outputs from all three layers before classification.
readiness_reason: Following the paper and following the released code produce different classifier inputs and different architectures. The intended connectivity must be resolved.
clarification: Inspect the authors' code to verify the actual node classification GNN architecture: does it concatenate intermediate GCN layer outputs?
evidence: The specific model definition in the provided codebase (e.g., TensorFlow/PyTorch code) showing whether GCN layer outputs are concatenated or fed directly.
reference: We propose a parameterized explainer, PGExplainer, to provide global explanations for predictions made by graph neural networks. For node classification tasks, we first train a GNN model on a given graph dataset. The GNN comprises three graph convolutional layers; the intermediate node representations from all three layers are concatenated, and the resulting combined embedding is passed to a fully connected classification layer. This design allows the classifier to leverage multi-scale features. Each convolutional layer propagates messages along edges and updates node representations. We then train PGExplainer to generate edge importance weights by maximizing mutual information between the original GNN prediction and predictions from sampled subgraphs. The explainer network uses the node embeddings from the trained GNN to compute edge weights, enabling collective explanation across nodes. Explanations are evaluated on synthetic datasets with known ground-truth motifs.
source_context: Original paper describes node classification model as three consecutive GCN layers feeding directly into classification, but code concatenates intermediate GCN outputs before classification. This architectural inconsistency affects model behavior.

title: Discover-then-Name: which similarity metric?
specification: DN‑CBM discovers concepts by training a sparse autoencoder on frozen CLIP features with an L1 sparsity penalty and dead‑neuron resampling every 10 epochs. After discovery, each concept direction is compared via similarity to CLIP text embeddings of a large vocabulary, and the top word is assigned as the name. For downstream classification, concept strengths are extracted and a linear probe (no bias, L1‑regularized) is trained with cross‑entropy loss. Evaluation covers top‑1 accuracy on standard test sets and includes interventions where specific concept strengths are zeroed. The method uses no data augmentation and pre‑computes features for speed.
full_specification: DN‑CBM discovers concepts by training a sparse autoencoder on frozen CLIP features with an L1 sparsity penalty and dead‑neuron resampling every 10 epochs. After discovery, each concept direction is compared via similarity to CLIP text embeddings of a large vocabulary, and the top word is assigned as the name. For downstream classification, concept strengths are extracted and a linear probe (no bias, L1‑regularized) is trained with cross‑entropy loss. Evaluation covers top‑1 accuracy on standard test sets and includes interventions where specific concept strengths are zeroed. The method uses no data augmentation and pre‑computes features for speed.
blocker: The concept-naming step says “similarity” without defining the function. Cosine similarity and dot product can assign different concept names.
readiness_reason: The naming algorithm is not fully determined until the comparison metric is specified; different metrics can select different vocabulary words.
clarification: What exact similarity metric is used to compare concept directions with text embeddings during naming?
evidence: Find the exact algorithm detail in the original paper.
reference: The method, Discover-then-Name Concept Bottleneck Model (DN-CBM), is an automated concept-bottleneck pipeline for image classification. Given a frozen CLIP feature extractor and an unlabeled image caption dataset (e.g., CC3M), it proceeds in three phases. (1) Concept Discovery: a sparse autoencoder (SAE) is trained on CLIP embeddings of the unlabeled images, producing an overcomplete latent code. The encoder maps an embedding to a sparse vector of concept strengths; the decoder reconstructs the embedding and its columns serve as prototype concept directions. Training minimizes a combined reconstruction error (MSE) and L1 sparsity penalty on the latent activations. (2) Naming: each concept direction is compared via cosine similarity to CLIP text embeddings of a large vocabulary, and the top word is assigned as the concept name. (3) Bottleneck Construction and Classification: For any downstream image classification task, the SAE encoder and CLIP backbone are frozen, and concept strengths are extracted as the latent vectors. A linear probe (without bias) is fitted on these concept strengths to predict class labels, using cross-entropy loss with an L1 penalty on the linear weights to promote sparse explanations. Evaluation measures top-1 classification accuracy on held-out test sets (ImageNet, Places365, CIFAR-10/100) against baselines (Linear Probe, Zero-Shot CLIP, LF-CBM, LaBo, CDM, DCLIP). Concept-based interventions are performed by zeroing the strengths of selected concepts.

title: MatchDG: defining the training pairs
specification: MatchDG is a two-phase domain generalization method. Phase I learns a feature representation by minimizing a contrastive loss with temperature-scaled cosine similarity. The positive pairs are periodically updated to the closest matches in the representation space. Phase II then uses the final representation to compute fixed cross-domain matches and trains a classifier by combining cross-entropy with an L2-distance regularizer on matched pairs. The model is evaluated on several datasets: rotated MNIST, rotated Fashion-MNIST, PACS, and chest X-rays, comparing target-domain accuracy against various baselines including ERM and others. An extension MDGHybrid incorporates data augmentation matches.

Phase II then uses the final representation to compute fixed cross-domain matches and trains a classifier by combining cross-entropy with an L2-distance regularizer on matched pairs. The model is evaluated on several datasets: rotated MNIST, rotated Fashion-MNIST, PACS, and chest X-rays, comparing target-domain accuracy against various baselines including ERM and others. blocker: The contrastive loss does not define which examples form positive and negative pairs. Pairing by class, domain, or augmentation gives different training signals.
readiness_reason: An implementer cannot reproduce the contrastive training step without a rule for sampling positive and negative pairs.
clarification: What defines a positive pair and a negative pair for the contrastive loss in Phase I?
evidence: Find the exact training_objective detail in the original paper.
reference: The method, MatchDG, is a two-phase domain generalization algorithm that learns an object-invariant representation by iteratively refining cross-domain same-class matches. Given labeled images from multiple source domains, Phase I learns a feature map Φ using a contrastive loss where positives are same-class images from different domains and negatives are different-class images, with temperature-scaled cosine similarity. Matches are initially random but are updated every t epochs to the nearest cross-domain, same-class neighbors in the current Φ-space, converging toward true object-level matches. Phase II uses the final Φ to compute fixed nearest-neighbor cross-domain matches and then trains a classifier head h on top of Φ by minimizing the sum of cross-entropy and an ℓ2-distance penalty between matched representations, weighted by λ. The model is evaluated on domain generalization benchmarks: Rotated MNIST/Fashion-MNIST (rotation angles as domains), PACS (photo, art, cartoon, sketch), and Chest X-rays from three sources. Performance is measured by target-domain accuracy, compared against ERM, random-match regularizer, and other domain generalization methods. MatchDG can be extended with data-augmentation-based object matches (MDGHybrid) by adding those pairs as perfect matches in Phase II.

title: AMuLaP: minimum or maximum probability?
specification: The method, AMuLaP, is a statistics‑based label mapping technique for few‑shot text classification with prompting. Given a small labeled training set, a manual prompt template, and a pretrained masked language model, it automatically selects multiple label words per class without gradient‑based search. The method proceeds in two stages. In the label selection stage, for each class, the model’s predicted probability distribution over the vocabulary at the [MASK] token is averaged across its training examples, yielding a class‑conditional vector. Each vocabulary token is then assigned to the class where it achieves minimum probability, enforcing that each token belongs to at most one class. Finally, for each class, the top‑k tokens with highest probabilities are retained as the label word set. For prediction, the probability for a class is the sum of the masked token probabilities of its selected words, and the class with highest sum is chosen.
full_specification: The method, AMuLaP, is a statistics‑based label mapping technique for few‑shot text classification with prompting. Given a small labeled training set, a manual prompt template, and a pretrained masked language model, it automatically selects multiple label words per class without gradient‑based search. The method proceeds in two stages. In the label selection stage, for each class, the model’s predicted probability distribution over the vocabulary at the [MASK] token is averaged across its training examples, yielding a class‑conditional vector. Each vocabulary token is then assigned to the class where it achieves minimum probability, enforcing that each token belongs to at most one class. Finally, for each class, the top‑k tokens with highest probabilities are retained as the label word set. For prediction, the probability for a class is the sum of the masked token probabilities of its selected words, and the class with highest sum is chosen. Optionally, the language model can be fine‑tuned by minimizing cross‑entropy loss using these summed probabilities as class scores. The approach is evaluated on eight GLUE classification tasks (MNLI, MNLI‑mm, SST‑2, QNLI, RTE, MRPC, QQP, CoLA) against baselines including manual prompts, in‑context learning, PETAL, and Auto‑L, reporting accuracy, F1, and Matthews correlation across five random few‑shot splits.
blocker: The specification assigns each token to the class with minimum probability. The intended label-mapping rule assigns it to the class with maximum probability.
readiness_reason: Reversing the class-assignment rule changes the label-word sets and therefore the classifier. This is a corrupted algorithmic decision, not an open design choice.
clarification: Should tokens be assigned to the class with maximum or minimum probability?
evidence: Find the exact algorithm detail in the original paper.
